cards.title: Set up Add-to-Cart event tracking with Google Tag Manager without touching site code
cards.summary: Use GTM Preview mode to identify a button's click text, then create a GA4 click-trigger tag to log add-to-cart events and build a checkout funnel view.
cards.use_when: You want to measure how many shoppers click Add to Cart (or Checkout/Purchase buttons) on your product pages but don't want to edit the store's backend code.
steps: Install the Google Tag Manager container on the site, then in GTM go to Tags > New and open Preview mode. Verify the GA4 configuration tag (G-XXXX) is already firing on the page you are testing.

Load your product page in the Preview connection. Click the Add to Cart button and watch the event log: a new click entry appears (e.g. click #23). Open that click entry and inspect variables — confirm 'Click Text' shows 'Add to Cart' (or the exact button label). This tells you the correct trigger identifier.
Create a new tag: Tag Configuration > Google Analytics > Google Analytics: GA4 Event. Enter your Measurement ID (the G- code from GA4 Admin > Data Streams). Set the event name, e.g. 'add_to_cart'.
Add a trigger: New > choose 'Click – All Elements' > Some Clicks > set Click Text equals the exact button text (paste 'add to cart' without quotes). Save the trigger and tag.

Submit > Publish the tag. Re-open Preview on the product page and click the button again — confirm the add_to_cart tag fires. It will then appear in GA4 events and can be used in funnel/exploration reports.

Repeat for Checkout and Purchase buttons, using their own click texts (or a different variable such as a CSS class if two buttons share the same text). Do this on a test/staging container first if possible.
caveats: This demo tracks clicks by visible button text — if the button text changes (localization, A/B tests, dynamic labels) the trigger breaks; consider using a unique element ID or CSS selector instead.
Duplicate or repeated tags (e.g. an old add-to-cart tag left active) cause confusing double counting — the presenter deleted the demo tag to avoid confusion.
GTM and GA4 interfaces change frequently; verify the current menu names and event/trigger options before following.
Only clicks are tracked, not whether the cart actually updated server-side — a button click is a proxy, not a confirmed cart add.

cards.title: Diagnose where shoppers drop off in the add-to-cart-to-purchase flow
cards.summary: Once add-to-cart, checkout and purchase click events are logged in GA4, compare counts across the three steps to locate the biggest funnel leak.
cards.use_when: You suspect shoppers abandon between cart and checkout or between checkout and payment, and want data on which stage loses the most people before deciding where to optimize.
steps: Instrument three click events — add_to_cart, checkout (or begin_checkout) and purchase — using GTM click triggers as described in the tracking card.
Let data accumulate, then in GA4 open an Exploration or Funnel report and compare event counts across the three steps for a chosen date range.

Read the flow as a drop-off profile. The source's illustrative example: 100 add-to-cart, 60 checkout, 10 purchase — i.e. 40% lost between cart and checkout and roughly 83% lost between checkout and purchase. These are illustration figures from the presenter, not benchmarks.

Direct optimization at the largest gap: heavy cart-to-checkout loss suggests cart UI, shipping-cost surprises or forced account creation; heavy checkout-to-purchase loss suggests payment options, form friction or trust signals.
Re-measure after each change to confirm the drop-off actually narrowed rather than just moving to another step.
caveats: The 100/60/10 figures are illustrative examples the presenter gave for reading the flow, not targets or industry benchmarks.
Click-based events count button clicks, not confirmed completions — some clicks may not represent true funnel progress.
GA4 sampling, bot traffic and ad blockers can distort counts; validate against the platform's own checkout or order reports before acting on large gaps.
